name: Vesugen

card.summary: A Lys-Glu-Asp tripeptide (KED) from Khavinson's lab pitched for blood vessels; cell-culture data, one small Russian human report, no appearance link.
card.note: Research peptide; evidence is mostly in vitro and from one research network.

quick.overview:
Vesugen is a three-amino-acid peptide (Lys-Glu-Asp) from the Khavinson bioregulator program, described as a vascular-protective agent.

Studies are mostly cell cultures. A Russian patent exists for a capillary-strengthening use, but no controlled human trial was found.
quick.mechanism: Reported to restore the proliferation marker Ki-67 in aged vascular cell cultures, apparently by interacting with its gene promoter in docking models [1]. Also reported to limit lipid peroxidation of lipoproteins in vitro [2].
quick.risks: No systematic human safety data; not an approved medicine.

lead: Vesugen is a synthetic tripeptide, Lys-Glu-Asp (KED, also called T-38), developed by Vladimir Khavinson's group and described as a vasoprotective peptide based on sequences from vascular-tissue extracts [3].

Published work is mostly in vitro: it was reported to restore the proliferation marker Ki-67 in aged endothelial and tissue cultures [1][1] and to restrict lipid peroxidation of human lipoproteins [2]. A Russian-language report examined synthetic peptides in elderly patients with brain syndrome [5]. It is not an approved drug and no appearance use is documented.
infobox: Russian patent RU 2295970 (2007) on capillary resistance [3]

paras: In aged tissue-specific and endothelial cell cultures, vesugen was reported to raise Ki-67 expression, with docking analysis suggesting interaction with the MKI67 promoter [1]. It was also reported to promote differentiation in aging cell cultures [6]. In vitro, vesugen and other short peptides lacked direct antioxidant activity but modified lipoprotein structure to limit lipid peroxidation and raised red-blood-cell membrane stability [2]. Another report describes short peptides' antihypoxic properties [7].

An AI-generated encyclopedia summary attributes vesugen to Khavinson's St. Petersburg institute in the late 1990s and early 2000s, and cites a 2007 Russian patent covering a peptide substance that increases capillary resistance [3].

No studies found specific to vesugen in controlled human trials. A Russian-language report on synthetic peptides in elderly patients with chronic polymorbidity and organic brain syndrome exists [5], but the sources reviewed do not allow attributing results to vesugen specifically.

timeline.event: Russian patent RU 2295970 granted for a capillary-strengthening peptide agent [3].
